sections.html:
The first step is the city's Point-of-Sale inspection, because a Certificate of Inspection has to exist before you sign a purchase agreement. That requirement sits on top of whichever sale route you choose: a traditional listing, a private sale, or a direct purchase from a cash buyer.

Cleveland Heights is an inner-ring suburb east of Cleveland, in Cuyahoga County, and it handles resale houses differently from many Ohio towns. The city wants to see the property's condition on paper before title moves, and it also wants the buyer to acknowledge that paper. Owners who plan around that sequence close smoothly. Owners who learn about it from a title company a week before closing often lose time.

A city inspector reviews the house and issues a Certificate of Inspection, which the seller must hand to the buyer before the sales contract is executed. The requirement covers single-family and two-family homes, duplexes, apartments, condominiums and commercial buildings.

  • Cost: $200 for the first unit and $50 for each additional unit, so a two-family house runs $250 and a four-unit building $350.
  • Shelf life: the certificate is valid for one year from the date it is issued. A Certificate of Compliance goes to the buyer as well, if one is available.
  • Booking: appointments are scheduled through the online portal on the city's site, and the Housing Inspections office is at 40 Severance Circle, phone 216-291-5900.
  • Paperwork: the buyer signs an acknowledgement form confirming receipt of the certificate.

The inspection checklist is posted online, so you can walk the house yourself first and see what an inspector will mark.

Escrow is required when a major Class A violation is still open at the time title transfers. Minor items on a well-kept house do not trigger it.

  • Outside: major concrete work, dead trees, downspouts tied to storm sewers, fences, big porch and step repairs, paint and the carpentry that goes with it, worn-out windows or doors, and roof or chimney work.
  • Inside: a bowed or collapsed foundation wall or post, heating and cooling systems, large breaches in ceilings, walls or floors, major plumbing repair, and major electrical repair such as a new panel.

Inspectional Services sets the dollar amount from average repair prices multiplied by 125% for an average-sized Cleveland Heights home. Typical figures are $6,250 for a roof and $5,625 for painting a single-family house, and your real cost may run higher or lower. You may instead submit a signed agreement with a contractor who is registered and bonded with the city, and the city may accept that estimate. A 203K, FNMA or similar rehab loan can stand in for cash if it covers every Class A item. Held funds are released only on written city authorization, and partial releases are possible once substantial progress is shown.

sections.h2: Getting the city's release before closing
sections.html:
Inspectional Services must receive three items and then send the title company a release letter. This applies to every sale in the city, whether or not escrow is owed.

Steps to release a Cleveland Heights property for transfer
StepWhat is submittedWho usually provides it
1Acknowledgement form signed by the buyerBuyer, collected by the seller or agent
2Title company name, escrow officer, address, phone and faxTitle company
3Letter stating the required escrow amount is held, if escrow appliesTitle company
4Release letter sent to the title companyInspectional Services

If the property is not released, a court summons may be issued. Send the first three items early, because the release letter is what lets the closing go forward.

The city sits on the Portage Escarpment, a ridge that gives the east side a higher elevation than downtown Cleveland. It covers about 8 square miles. The first road through the area, Mayfield Road, was built in 1828, and the place became a city on August 9, 1921, growing mostly in the streetcar era. Many houses date from that early boom, and the Euclid Golf Allotment is on the National Register of Historic Places. Coventry Village is the best-known shopping street.

The 2025 estimate is 43,750 residents, down 3.5% from the April 2020 base. Owners live in 58.2% of homes, a far higher share than in neighboring Cleveland. The median owner-occupied home value is $192,100 on the 2020-2024 survey, and median gross rent is $1,216. There are 19,323 households, and a 2020 census tally found 22,270 housing units with 10.0% vacant.

Most of the city belongs to the Cleveland Heights-University Heights City School District, which has six elementary schools inside city limits, two middle schools and Cleveland Heights High School. A small northwest corner lies in the East Cleveland City School District. Buyers ask about district boundaries, so tell your agent or your buyer which district your street falls in.

The land rises quickly east of the lake, and the Heights lie where the Snow Belt begins, so seasonal snowfall approaching 100 inches is not unusual there. Lake-effect snow typically runs from mid-November until Lake Erie freezes in late January or early February.

That climate explains why the city's Class A list names roofs, chimneys, downspouts, paint and windows. If you have an older roof or peeling exterior paint, expect the inspector to flag it and plan for either the repair or the escrow.

sections.h2: Cuyahoga County steps after you agree on a price
sections.html:
Cuyahoga County's Fiscal Office handles transfer and recording at 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, in Cleveland, with office hours Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and recording hours ending at 4:00 p.m. Every transfer must come with either the DTE 100 statement of value or the DTE 100-EX exemption statement. The standard recording fee is $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after that, under Senate Bill 94. Call 216-443-2060 with questions.

Property tax is billed separately. Ohio's House Bill 920 of 1976 lowers a district's effective rate as values climb during reappraisals, and the Cuyahoga County Treasurer posts rates by community. Ask the Fiscal Office or your closing agent for the current figure on your parcel.

Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 also asks most sellers of homes with one to four units to give the buyer a signed property disclosure form, with exceptions for estates, inheritors who never lived there and transfers between family members in a direct line.

faqs.q: Can I accept an offer before the Point-of-Sale inspection is done?
faqs.a: No. The city requires the Certificate of Inspection before you enter into an agreement to sell, and the buyer receives a copy before the contract is executed. Book the inspection first, then list or negotiate.

faqs.q: What happens if repairs are not finished by closing?
faqs.a: Major Class A violations still open at transfer require escrowed funds, set at 125% of average repair prices for an average-sized home. A signed contract with a city-registered, bonded contractor, or a rehab loan covering every Class A item, may be accepted in place of cash.

faqs.q: How long does a Cleveland Heights Certificate of Inspection last?
faqs.a: It is valid for one year from the date of issuance. If your house sits unsold for longer than that, a new inspection is needed before you sign a contract.

faqs.q: Which school district serves my Cleveland Heights house?
faqs.a: Most addresses are in the Cleveland Heights-University Heights City School District. A small area on the northwest side belongs to the East Cleveland City School District, so check your street before you describe the schools.

faqs.q: Where is a Cleveland Heights deed recorded?
faqs.a: At the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office, 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, Cleveland. The deed needs a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX form, and your title company normally files both.
